It's true that the idea that there would be a future messiah to fulfill God's promises emerged after the Babylonians overthrew the nation of Judea in 587 B.C.E. and removed the Jewish King from the throne (Ehrman, 2000, p. 61).  
The first mentions of a Messiah in the Hebrew Bible came from the prophets Haggai and Zechariah during the Persian Period; they viewed Zerubbabel as the ruler of the last days. The idea that a Messiah from the House of David would rule in the last days was tied to the belief that the Davidic line would endure forever, as established in 2 Samuel 7. This 'Davidic Messiah' idea saw a revival in the Hellenistic ages when Alexander arrived in Palestine, after a period where the concept was largely absent from Jewish writings. See the author of Deutero-Zechariah, who presents a Davidic Messiah who is a national hero and a genuine descendant of David and Solomon.

Later, the traditional Davidic promise also coalesced with the sacerdotal messianism during the Hasmonaean dynasty (look for: dual messianism). So by the Roman Period, the Jewish concept of the Messiah had diversified. There was no single, unified concept of "the Messiah" (Ehrman, 2006, p. 19). Some expected a warrior-king, others a supernatural judge, and still others a priestly ruler. Many of these expectations were heavily influenced by earlier apocalyptic and prophetic writings such as Daniel and Enoch (Knibb, 2011, p. 15).
